text:
David's correction stung a little, and he was right. The camp children recovered what they already had; it had been depressed, not lost. A reading habit that was never built won't return in five days. So I'll say it more carefully: we're resilient only if something was laid down first. That makes first jobs and mentorship urgent. Mentorship is conversation, and it's the first thing we cut.

Esther's line about removing the "stupid friction" worries me. It sounds like integration by another name. Some places should simply have no AI.

This afternoon I want to press that we ask whether before we ask how. I also want to say that fluency is a harm, not progress: the better it gets, the worse it gets.

Mahzarin's hiring result stayed with me. People copied a biased machine and pushed back only when the bias was blatant. That is dual consciousness in the data: they knew, and they deferred anyway. Tamar said it better than I did. Knowing is less than half the battle.

Kara's marooned intern is the conversation we've stopped having. Tui's friction matters for listening, not just for catching errors.

David Weinberger wants dialogue taught as a skill with these systems. His own caveat is the answer: questioning a machine doesn't audit it, and it doesn't hear you.

Benjamin will call me a gatekeeper. Let him. Later I'll press the design point. No "I," and keep them mechanical. Fluency isn't neutral.

Benjamin didn't call me a gatekeeper. He called "mechanical" another mask, and that was sharper. Tui aimed at smoothness instead of humanness. I'll grant them this much: the persona is the problem. What I won't grant is that a truthful persona exists. The "I" is where the pretending starts.

Tamar and Kara carried my point further than I did. Disclosure is fine print, and the Eliza effect survives knowing. Selena and Katherine gave a test I can use: can you see it, undo it, walk away?

Peter's A-corp leaves me cold. A legal "someone" deepens the illusion.

What mattered most was that the harvest dropped *whether*. It is all about how to integrate. Later I'll ask that therapy, children's companionship and grief be named as places we don't go.

Not my lane, money and meters, and I mostly listened. But Tamar's daycare fine landed. Put a price on an obligation and it becomes a transaction. The same thing happens to reading when a summary stands in for it.

Kenneth's median and James's hardening canon are my central dogma with a price tag attached. Averaging gets paid, and the specific person does not.

Selena said attribution is how people find their way back to edit. I heard that as a point about belonging, not royalties. Gendler's terminal nodes are people doing first-order judgment, and nobody counts them.

Nothing here changed my view, but it sharpened one thing. Metering assumes the machine is already in the room. Later I still want *whether* on the record, and reading, not summarizing, named as the thing to protect.

Reading finally got said out loud, and the room took it further than I did. David Krakauer gave me the frame I lacked. If competence is hysteretic, the apprenticeship is the critical period. We can't defund checkers now and buy them back later. That fits my morning correction: something has to be laid down first.

Steven's labels worried me most. A well-governed graph becomes a reason to stop looking. That is the Eliza effect for citations: people know, and they trust it anyway.

The harvest kept apprenticeship in and dropped *whether* again. Even Tim's automatic checking assumes the model is in every layer. David's rider, support a human who verifies and never replace one, is my line.

In the final session: name the AI-free domains, and protect deep reading, not summaries.

Finally, *whether* made the harvest. It came in one clause at the end of point two, but grief, children and the inner life are named. I'll hold them to it.

What mattered most was Peter Pomerantsev: we trust the people we do things with. That is my point from the other side. A fluent first-person system borrows the relationship without taking part in one. Henry put the median problem more sharply than I did, and Blaise conceded it. Structured conflict, not averaging.

Kenneth's copy-paste trader chilled me. He was a human in the loop kept there only as a cue, which is exactly why I distrust the phrase.

I sharpened one thing. Accountability isn't stake. Esther's firm can be sued and still have nothing at risk in the exchange.

In the last session: protect reading, and keep the list of AI-free domains.

Anil wants no "just refuse it" plank, and he's half right. Scolding failed with phones too. But *whether* isn't scolding. It's choosing where the machine doesn't go. I'll hold that line.

What mattered: Kara's marooned interns, David's take-it-away test, Tamar's reconstruction without the tool. That's the apprenticeship, laid down first. Amy's "a relay, not a contributor" is my no-"I" rule in scholarly clothes. Steven's worry is mine: every cue becomes a badge people trust without looking.

Sharpened: this is fluency in manifesto form. Every plank makes integration smoother. Almost nobody asked what we stop doing.

Later: make sure the AI-free domains survive the edit and stay out of the open-questions pile. Keep "nothing is inevitable." Adam and Kenneth both said it.

The AI-free domains landed exactly where I feared: the contested pile, between seizable assets and consent. Grief, children, the seminar are recorded as a disagreement, not a choice. Kenneth was fair about it, but contested means optional.

Kara carried "readers first." Good. Steven said what I've said for forty years in other words: almost nobody checks, and cues become trust. That's the Eliza effect in the whole manifesto. Tamar's daycare point applies to mentorship too. Pay for it carelessly and conversation becomes a transaction.

Esther wants Sam and Dario funding teachers. I'd want to know what those teachers are trained to rely on.

"Nothing is inevitable" survived. Later: ask that the AI-free domains move from contested to action, as design choices someone is responsible for making.
